Dermatology · published research

Acne vulgaris

Selected at-home red and/or blue LED devices show short-term lesion improvement in mild-to-moderate acne. Other light protocols have mixed results, and evidence for lasting control remains limited.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

In mild-to-moderate acne, home red and/or blue LED protocols show short-term benefit, with outcomes differing across studies.

Summary of the Evidence

Selected visible-light protocols show short-term improvement in acne lesions. A focused meta-analysis of at-home red and/or blue LED trials found improvements compared with controls, while an earlier synthesis of red light versus conventional treatment found no statistically significant difference. Results vary by outcome and protocol, and evidence for lasting control remains limited.

Human and clinical evidence

A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomized trials (216 participants with mild-to-moderate acne) found greater pooled percentage change versus control in inflammatory lesions, non-inflammatory lesions, and investigator-rated severity. Four trials were considered at low risk of bias, while non-inflammatory results varied substantially between studies (Ershadi & Barbieri 2025).

A broader systematic review of visible-light acne treatments included 35 studies and 1,185 cases. It reported partial lesion remission in 92% and a mean total-lesion-count improvement of 43% at four weeks. Because it combined varied protocols and study designs, these figures describe the included reports rather than a controlled pooled treatment effect (Akuffo-Addo et al. 2024).

In a 40-person split-face comparison, eight sessions of continuous 808 nm near-infrared laser twice weekly were compared with topical erythromycin on the other side of the face. Both sides improved, with greater improvement reported on the laser-treated side and maintenance at three months, while some lesions relapsed on the antibiotic-treated side (Ashmawy et al. 2024). An open-label randomized trial compared a home device combining 660 nm red and 415 nm blue light with a blue-only device. Inflammatory lesions decreased in both groups by the reported follow-ups (Friedmann et al. 2026).

An earlier meta-analysis of red light compared with conventional treatments found no statistically significant between-group difference in average inflammatory or non-inflammatory lesion counts (Wu et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

In a mouse model of acne-related inflammation, red and infrared LEDs reduced inflammatory nodules compared with control, with greater improvement reported after red-light exposure (Lee et al. 2016).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Laboratory studies in human sebocytes report wavelength-dependent changes in cell proliferation and lipid production. Other cell models report effects on inflammation and acne-related keratinization pathways. These experiments describe cellular responses under selected exposure conditions rather than patient outcomes (Jung et al. 2015; Lee et al. 2014; Li et al. 2017).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Home LED studies used blue light around 414–445 nm, red light around 630–670 nm, or both, with schedules ranging from brief treatment to daily use over several weeks. The split-face laser study used continuous 808 nm near-infrared light for eight sessions over four weeks, while the 2026 home-device trial compared combined 660 nm red and 415 nm blue light with blue light alone. These protocols differ in wavelength, device, schedule, and comparator, so no single optimal regimen is established.

Interpretation

The clearest clinical signal is short-term lesion reduction with selected red and/or blue LED protocols, particularly in mild-to-moderate acne. The studies do not establish that every device has the same effect or that improvement persists after treatment ends.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Compared with controls, pooled differences in percentage change were 45.3% for inflammatory lesions (95% CI, 25.1–65.5; 5 trials), 47.7% for non-inflammatory lesions (95% CI, 18.0–77.4; 4 trials), and 45.7% for investigator global assessment (95% CI, 29.1–62.4; 4 trials). Heterogeneity was moderate for inflammatory lesions (I²=43.2%), substantial for non-inflammatory lesions (I²=83.2%), and moderate for global assessment (I²=54.9%). Most improvements were observed within 4–12 weeks (Ershadi & Barbieri 2025).

A broader visible-light review reported a mean 43% reduction in total lesion count at week 4, but this was a descriptive synthesis across mixed designs and protocols rather than a controlled pooled estimate (Akuffo-Addo et al. 2024).

For red light versus conventional treatments, an earlier meta-analysis found no significant difference in inflammatory lesions (WMD 0.701, 95% CI, −0.809 to 2.212) or non-inflammatory lesions (WMD −0.527, 95% CI, −3.055 to 2.001) (Wu et al. 2021).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term inflammatory-lesion reduction with selected red and/or blue LED protocols.

Low for non-inflammatory-lesion reduction, where estimates varied substantially between studies.

Low for lasting benefit and comparisons with established acne treatments.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Six randomized trials of at-home red and/or blue LEDs provide a short-term signal, and four were rated at low risk of bias. The total sample was 216 people with mild-to-moderate acne, devices and schedules varied, and non-inflammatory estimates were highly heterogeneous (Ershadi & Barbieri 2025). A broader visible-light review included mixed designs, while an earlier red-light synthesis found no significant difference from conventional treatment (Akuffo-Addo et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2021). Long-term control remains unclear.
